records.title: Show HN: New In browser URL verification tool
records.author: integrity_softw
records.storyText:
This is an in web browser address bar URL authenticity verification tool using only a special redirection system attached to the subdomains of trustedurl.org

For example, to check the authenticity of and visit the authenticated site, add .trustedurl.org after the Top-Level Domain.

>getmonero.org.trustedurl.org

Entered into the address bar, this resolves to

>getmonero.org

You can also just type in the domain name without the TLD

>getmonero.trustedurl.org

Which similarily resolves to

>https://getmonero.org

This of course also works with the protocol

>https://getmonero.org.trustedurl.org >https://getmonero.trustedurl.org

Now say an attacker were to make a phishing site getphished.org, and you were uncertain if it were authentic. In this case, just apply the same postfix to the suspect domain

>getphished.org.trustedurl.org

Which resolves to a connection error page, because it isn't in the authentic URL whitelist.

So far only a few cryptocurrency exchanges simpleswap.io, trocador.app, bisq and wallets bitcoin.org, electrum.org, getmonero.org have been added to the whitelist, along with torproject.org, i2p.net, freenet.org, devuan.org, tails.net

SimpleSwap cryptocurrency exchange >simpleswap.trustedurl.org >simpleswap.io.trustedurl.org

TAILS OS >tails.trustedurl.org >tails.net.trustedurl.org

Monero wallet >getmonero.org.trustedurl.org >getmonero.trustedurl.org

There are many fake websites and URLs that closely resemble the real sites, and going on the wrong site can easily lead to getting scammed of money and downloading malware. Using this tool prevents this by providing an extra layer of security if one hasn't memorized the exact fully qualified domain.

records.title: Show HN: a Rust implementation of the Reticulum mesh networking stack
records.author: aaaljaz
records.storyText:
This is a fork of original rust sdk from https://github.com/BeechatNetworkSystemsLtd/Reticulum-rs/ that I extended significantly to make it fully feature compatible with the reference implementation that is built in python. I wanted to expand the rust sdk to give me full toolbox and easy way to do bindings for different languages including for building mobile apps.

it covers the full surface: pathfinding and announce propagation, links, requests, resource transfers(bzip2, same wire format), identity ratchets, tunnels, LXMF messaging with propagation sync, serial/KISS/AX.25, RNode (incl. BLE), IPv6 auto-peering and I2P interfaces, Kotlin and Swift bindings so mobile apps can embed the stack directly.

CLI tools (rnstatus, rnpath, rnsh, rnx) are ported too.

I've done some experiments with it liek creating a LoRa chat firmware for the M5Stack Cardputer and a full node/repeater for M5Stack Unit C6L to have a tiny reticulum node with full stack

Before anyone gives me shit - I've opened an upstream PR but given the size of the change I'dnt blame them for not wanting to deal with it.

records.storyText:
I've always loved flipbooks, the little stick figure running and jumping around the corner of a page. I was curious if I could hi-jack a font file with stick figure glyphs. So I prompted Flipbook Foundry into existence.

Each animated frame of the a stick figure's motion is just a glyph in the font. You can drop {walk} into a paragraph and a stick figure walks right through it, at text size, and the words move aside.

The text reflow runs on Cheng Lou's awesome pretext library, which is fast enough to animate everything performantly.

There's an API for it (framer-motion style, for Svelte / React / plain JS), and the fonts are regular .otf files. Made a little demo page too - check it out and enjoy the swarm!

records.title: Show HN: Hello Triangle, a puzzle game where you build a GPU
records.author: icedlatte
records.storyText:
I've been working on a game Hello Triangle for a while. In the game, you build a GPU one part at a time by wiring circuits, and renders a picture on the screen with what your circuit computes. I have a free demo available that goes up to drawing a triangle, while I'm still working on the rest of the game.

You don't start from logic gates. The game starts with adders and comparators. Every wire just carries a fixed point number, and there are no bit widths to think about. The reason of using fixed point numbers is that veteran players of Turing Complete can skip the bits part they already player, while players who are new to programming can still jump right in.

The circuit simulator is written in Go and the game UI is written in Godot, and they communitate through stdio. I also built a score server that players can upload their scores and compare with each other through score histograms.

The demo is available on Steam (Windows/macOS/Linux), there's also an itch.io build if you don't use Steam. Curious what you think, and where you get stuck!

records.author: fraywing
records.storyText:
Howdy HN!

Inspired by StarSkirmish, I wanted to build a complex RTS that required you to bring your OWN agents and either play with them as allies, against them as enemies, or battle head-to-head with other agent-human pairs in public matches.

In AC you operate one or more planes (Orbit, Sky, Surface, Depths) of differing gameplay. As an old-school PC gamer I wanted the mechanics to resemble some of my favorite 90s games of yore: C&C, DungeonKeeper, Homeworld, StarCraft, and others. The idea is that you have specific objectives needed to maximize resource generation, aid in cross player support, and that a single plane cannot win independently.

Outside of gameplay, from an agentic tech pov, there are some other really cool things that come with this, including:

- A full specification + library to install agents into any game (http://playerthree.gg/) - A networking SDK for bidirectional agent communication - Symmetric maps - Deterministic simulation - Benchmarking tools - (soon) published benchmark data

Github: https://github.com/agent-command/agent-command Play now: https://agentcommand.gg/

Would love feedback and contribs if interested in RTS games and AI!

records.title: Show HN: Althar – an open-source IDE where agents review each other's work
records.author: itsbalazs
records.storyText:
Hey HN, I'm Balázs, and I wanted to share my passion project that I've been building in my free time. It is free, it is open-source, and I've poured a lot of love into making it delightful.

I've spent a lot of time dabbling with agentic ADEs and IDEs since the days of the early VSCode forks. I've switched IDEs more times than I can count. Cursor. Copilot. Codex. PearAI. Orca. Claude Code. OpenCode. Superset. Agent Orchestrator. Windsurf, and then Devin. OpenChamber. Kilo. IntelliJ and VSCode plugins.

This September, I felt sort of stranded. I kept switching tools, losing all my chats, losing time, and frankly, losing love for the very thing that has been getting me out of bed every morning for the past decade. Programming. Building. Tinkering. I've spent more time fighting my tools, being forced back into terminals, being rug-pulled by labs, or being forced into the cloud, when really, I just want to work on my machine.

It was then that I started to jot down my frustrations in a blog post. Not that anyone would read it, especially these days, but my frustrations, I felt, needed an outlet. As I was writing the post, I sort of realised: for the longest time, I'd been observing and obsessing over products like Linear. Raycast. Arc. Their level of detail. Their thoughtful approach to UX. Their grassroots, scratch-a-boring-itch story.

So I decided to scratch my itch, and build an IDE that would stay out of your way. It's called Althar. Delightful to use, calm, and open, rethinking the old paradigms that are holding most of the industry captive. There's no sidebar. There's no built-in text editor. There are no chats (in a traditional sense).

Agents forgetting my project between tasks always annoyed me. So did my overarching goals and milestones getting lost between chats, and agents having no way to coordinate work with one another. In most tools I've tried, they work in silos.

So, in Althar, you organise your work in projects. A project can be a single repository, or many. On top of it sits your project manager, called the coordinator. You talk to her like you would talk to any PM on a project. You could say something like, "Help me make my website responsive and accessible. Also, help me measure the performance with Lighthouse." She will then split the work into three separate tasks, brief individual task agents called leads, assign each task a reviewer agent (we love a second opinion, but it's optional), and send them on their way.

Finished work comes back to you with screenshots, test evidence, and the reviewer's findings settled.

You see everything that's happening on a kanban-like board (though it is NOT kanban), and you're only pulled in when you're actually needed. No need to anxiously watch over terminals and in-flight agent thinking trails.

You can use all of your existing subscriptions. Claude. Codex. OpenCode and so on. It connects to your issue trackers and git hosts, wherever they may be.

Work happens locally. Next week, I hope to add support for remote runners, and I'm also working on a mobile companion.

I hope you'll enjoy it. There is so much to say, so many little details. But it's also early days, so please, if you do find issues, let me know :) Or open a pull request. The open source community has given me so much over the years. It is the best thing about software engineering, and something unique to our profession. I'm excited that I get to give back.

records.title: Show HN: SecureVibe – Find and trace vulnerabilities before shipping
records.author: Abdo2026
records.storyText:
Hello HN, just wanted to share my project that I've been working on the past months, where I noticed the issue that now we ship faster than setting up the requirements for the project. So I thought of building secureVibe to find vulnerabilities in your codebase.

Now I have a MVP where it doesn't just scan the code and show random analysis I used Tree-sitter and AST to understand code context to validate vulnerabilities found as it builds a graph of application routes, handlers and database calls so it helps to determine whether findings are confirmed or likely.

Briefly the features: 1- shows all vulnerabilities in your code with code snippets

2-fixing with ai option (optional with your own api key for now)

3- ask the graph feature as you can ask where the attacker can exploit my website or authentication issues (I used graphify as foundation for it )

4- You can filter vulnerabilities categories (like Cwe, database injection and more) from dashboard and you can download it as html report simple interactive one so you can fix it on your own later.

I would love to know your thoughts and feedback to continue on the development on it like some of the problems I faced is benchmarks to validate security rules. With some research I found openssf benchmark

On the OpenSSF CVE benchmark, the raw F1 score was 77.5, but still I face some issues with false positive

so would really appreciate feedback to continue on developing with next phases.

Even though with these issues Its still working well, it is efficient and fast and preferably start with TypeScript repos first for it.

I use Kuma for a few microservices I’ve built. It’s a simple open source tool for monitoring APIs, ports, websites etc if they are down.

The issue I get is that they are hosted on your own infrastructure, so it doesn’t do you a whole lot of good if your site is down and it takes your Kuma down with it. This also leads to a bunch of false notifications which are annoying.

From what I can tell, people in the GitHub comments are looking for hosted Kuma.

I built DownForReal (largely with LLMs) but what it does is it hosts Kuma and if Kuma is reporting the service down, probes from US, Frankfurt, and Singapore are sent to confirm the outage (looking for 2 out of 3 of the regions).

I’m asking $10 a month or $75 a year.

I’m really just launching this as a service bc I built it for myself.

There is also a simple importer for uptimerobot exports.

records.title: Show HN: Blaris – Windowless Random-Access LZSS for Constrained Microcontrollers
records.author: lis05
records.storyText:
Hello HN!

I'd like to share the project I've been working on for the last couple of months.

On microcontrollers with only a few kilobytes of memory (both Flash and SRAM) heatshrink [1] and tamp [2] are the current meta when it comes to decompression of static assets. They are small, configurable, and produce good compression ratio.

However, when random-access workflows are concerned (like extracting a single parameter from a configuration file), both compressors require the exact same window to be allocated. This means that, to decompress a small (4-32 bytes) chunk, memory consumption stays the same as when decompression the entire payload.

blaris is a Windowless LZSS algorithm, meaning that it is LZSS but does not allocate a window. This allows it to reach the same compression ratio (and sometimes even better) as heatshrink and tamp, while keeping memory usage extremely minimal (around 100 bytes of SRAM).

Typical LZ77/LZSS works by copying a byte from the window buffer when resolving a match. Windowless version works by resolving this match using the compressed payload itself - following the chain of matches until it finds a literal run token.

To facilitate this, tokens are split into 3 streams:

1. controls (1 byte per value) - encode either literal run length (1 to 16) or 240 different pairs (match_len, match_distance_log2).

2. literals (1 byte per value) - raw literals.

3. distance bits (bit-packed) - contains bit-packed match offsets.

Because controls are 1 byte and determine the size of the token, we can traverse all 3 streams in both directions, which enables the windowless LZSS!

There are additional optimizations used to speed this up:

1. checkpoints contain decoder state at each 2^SPREAD_LOG positions, which enables the decoder to jump to the closest checkpoint in constant time.

2. matches' offsets can be forced to align to a power of two, increasing the match range paying the price of unaligned matches.

3. optimal parser on compression side comes up with the best possible representation of the input.

4. chain-flattening can significantly reduce average number of match to match hops while sacrificing just 1-2% of the compression ratio.

When decompressing small slices (4-32 bytes), blaris significantly outperforms both heatshrink and tamp (500x for 1B reads). For bigger slices, since its decompression time depends linearly on the data, blaris performs worse, but it isn't really made for that.

And the best part, it is extremely lightweight in terms of memory. When compiled for RV32IMC architecture, it takes only 548-784 bytes of Flash memory, while using just 104-112B of SRAM regardless of the file size. For comparison, heatshrink is 1300-1464 bytes of Flash and uses 206-16594 bytes of SRAM depending on the window size, and tamp is 2238-3238 bytes of Flash while also using 520-16672 bytes of SRAM.

[1] https://github.com/atomicobject/heatshrink

[2] https://github.com/BrianPugh/tamp

records.title: Show HN: What HN community recommended learning in 2026
records.author: matyyyy
records.storyText:
Hi HN!

I've been software engineer for about 15 years. For me this industry was always about learning. To be honest, I don't feel this anymore. I see more and more people delegating most of their work to LLMs. We rarely talk about software design or architecture, because Claude is such a great companion, so most of the workers don't need these technical discussions.

Sometimes I feel a bit lost. I am not sure, what should I learn to stay in the industry and to have opportunity to work on interesting problems.

I always saw HN as a place full of ambitious and creatives people. Inspired by hackertube.org and hackerbooks.org, I scanned HN comments in 2026 to extract learning materials recommended by community here, to help me decide with the next steps in my learning journey.

Best, Mateusz
